title: The life-cycle comparison bureau
subtitle: Use shared features without making a false rule
objective: Compare named animal life cycles using similarities, differences and a valid counterexample.

sow.exactOutcome: Compare the life cycles of different living things.
sow.alignment: Intentional deeper comparison after grow_life_cycle_archive; use new evidence and questions. Original secondary-age exemplar at an upper-KS2 conceptual level; no qualification approval or completion claim.

priorLearning: Describe a named animal life cycle.
Know that adults can reproduce and offspring grow.
success: Compare two species using the same feature.
Use a life-cycle stage as evidence for a difference.
Explain why one shared feature does not make two animals the same group.

vocabulary.meaning: Describe similarities and differences using the same feature.
An immature stage with a different body form from the adult.
A developmental stage between larva and adult in insects with complete metamorphosis.
An animal in the group whose females produce milk for young.
A case that shows an all-or-never claim is false.

equipment: Shared species cards, selected route, pencils; optional desk sorting labels.
preparation: Read the named-species cards; no observations of live animals are required.
Explain that the diagrams omit exact times and are not to scale.
safety: Use the paper archive; do not collect eggs, disturb nests or handle wildlife.
practicalAlternative: All evidence needed is on paper or screen; sort or annotate cards at a desk.

misconceptions.claim: All animals that lay eggs are birds.
misconceptions.correction: Many other animals lay eggs; a platypus is an egg-laying mammal.
misconceptions.check: Ask which card provides a counterexample.

misconceptions.claim: A pupa is just another word for any baby animal.
misconceptions.correction: A pupa is a particular stage in insects such as monarch butterflies.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a frog has a pupa.

misconceptions.claim: An adult turns back into its own egg.
misconceptions.correction: Adults produce a new generation; an individual does not become an egg again.
misconceptions.check: Ask whose life starts at the next egg.

access.supported: Compare two named species with a feature word bank.
access.standard: Complete a feature table and justify one similarity and two differences.
access.stretch: Test broad classification claims and state the limits of the sample.
access.regulation: Offer private writing, pointing, drawing or adult scribing. Allow pass-and-return for public questions and desk-based participation. Choose support from current learning evidence, not fixed ability labels.

slides.title: Four cases, one comparison challenge
body: All four animals lay eggs.
Does that make all four birds?
Your job is to test the claim with evidence.
slides.notes: Invite a tentative response. No need to know the platypus in advance: the shared card supplies the needed evidence.

slides.title: Use the stage words carefully
body: R1. What does an adult animal become able to do?
R2. Name an animal with a larva stage.
R3. Does one individual turn back into an egg?
slides.notes: R1 reproduce; R2 monarch, common frog or another accurate example; R3 no, the next generation starts with new offspring.

slides.title: I choose a feature, then compare
body: I follow the common-frog stages.
A tadpole and adult differ in body form.
I look for a pupa; none is present.
slides.notes: Think aloud: I compare the presence of a pupa, not whether the animal is attractive or large. The frog route includes a larva and major change, but no pupa. Time spans and detailed anatomy are omitted.

slides.title: I use the same feature for the monarch
body: Both routes include eggs and a larva.
Only this monarch route has a pupa.
A shared stage does not make the whole cycle identical.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Think aloud: I use a matching question: Is a pupa present? For the monarch, yes; for common frog, no. This is a justified difference. Do not generalise the monarch route to every insect.

slides.title: I test an “all” claim
body: Platypus and robin both lay eggs.
Platypus young receive milk; robin chicks do not.
The platypus disproves “all egg-layers are birds”.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Explain a counterexample as one real case that breaks the rule. Mammal classification does not depend solely on live birth. Compare named species; do not infer every detail about all mammals from one.

visual.title: Eggs do not mean the same animal group
visual.description: Parallel comparisons of platypus and robin: both lay eggs, but platypus young receive milk and robin chicks receive food from parents. No arrow connects the animal groups.

slides.title: Comparison bureau: shared-feature sort
body: Use cards F, M, P and R.
W1. Group them by one feature, then regroup.
Explain why the groups changed.
slides.notes: First group by pupa: M yes; F/P/R no. Then milk feeding: P yes; F/M/R no. All four share egg-laying. Accept desk sorting, pointing or writing.

rows: Is this stage in the route?

slides.title: Build a precise comparison
body: W2. Compare common frog with monarch.
Give one similarity and one difference.
Use “both”, “whereas” or a labelled pair.
slides.notes: Both lay eggs and have larvae; monarch has pupa whereas frog does not. Do not accept merely different colours or sizes unsupported by cards.

slides.title: The claim challenge
body: W3. “All egg-layers are birds.”
Select a counterexample and explain it.
Can four species describe every animal?
slides.notes: Platypus, frog or monarch disproves claim; platypus specifically demonstrates an egg-laying mammal. Four examples do not describe all species. Reveal after pupil reasoning.
slides.reveal: The platypus lays eggs and is a mammal. That one case breaks the “all birds” claim.

slides.title: Which comparison uses evidence fairly?
body: Choose the statement that the cards support.
slides.notes: A false identical cycles. B correct feature-based comparison. C false all mammals live birth.

options.text: Frog and monarch have identical life cycles because both lay eggs.
options.feedback: Shared eggs do not erase differences such as the pupa stage.

options.text: Frog and monarch both have larvae, but only the monarch has a pupa.
options.feedback: The same stages are compared using both cards.

options.text: A platypus cannot be a mammal because it lays eggs.
options.feedback: The platypus is an egg-laying mammal and its young receive milk.

slides.title: Your independent investigation
body: Choose one response route.
Build an evidence-based comparison.
Test one broad claim with a named case.
slides.notes: 10 minutes across the three You do slides. Supply shared page 1 and one selected route page. All routes target the stated science objective; a labelled drawing or independent dictated explanation is valid.

slides.title: Use the evidence
body: Use the same feature for both animals.
Name your species and evidence card.
Distinguish “these examples” from “all animals”.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask pupils which evidence supports their explanation. Read prompts or scribe without supplying the scientific conclusion.

slides.title: Check before sharing
body: Does my explanation answer the question?
Have I named the evidence or process?
Have I kept the conclusion within its limits?
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Use the route-specific worked answers to identify one precise next step.

slides.title: Compare and improve
body: Show a precise similarity or difference.
Check the named evidence.
Improve one broad or vague statement.
slides.notes: 4 minutes across Review. Offer partner or private teacher feedback. Ask for one specific revision linked to evidence; no public ranking.

slides.title: A question worth investigating
body: Suggest one next question about this lesson’s evidence.
Choose a question whose answer would improve our model.
slides.notes: Lundy cycle: invite written, spoken or pointed suggestions. Select one feasible question and explain how the pupil contribution changes the next example or investigation.

slides.title: Show the science you can explain
body: E1. Give a frog–monarch similarity.
E2. Give one difference in stages.
E3. Explain a counterexample to “all egg-layers are birds”.
slides.notes: Eggs/larvae shared; pupa only monarch; any named non-bird egg-layer with accurate reason. E4 on page asks about the next generation.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: comparison bureau
pupilPages.intro: Named-species summaries. Use these cards for W1–W3 and your selected route.

cards.title: F • Common frog
cards.text: Eggs are laid in pond water. Tadpoles are larvae with tails; they develop into froglets and then adults. No pupa stage. No milk feeding.

cards.title: M • Monarch butterfly
cards.text: Eggs are laid on milkweed. Caterpillars are larvae; they become pupae, then adult butterflies. No milk feeding.

cards.title: P • Platypus
cards.text: A mammal that lays eggs in a burrow. The young hatch and receive milk from their mother; they grow to reproductive maturity. No pupa.

cards.title: R • Robin
cards.text: A bird that lays eggs in a nest. Chicks hatch, grow feathers and become fledglings, then reproductive adults. Parents bring food; no milk feeding.

cards.title: Comparison rule
cards.text: Use the same feature on both sides: egg location, pupa stage, or milk feeding. A blank in our evidence means not supplied, not automatically absent.

cards.title: Cycle rule
cards.text: Adults produce offspring. The next eggs belong to a new generation; the same individual does not turn back into an egg.

blocks.prompt: W1. Group the four species by pupa stage, then by milk feeding. Why do groups change?
W2. Compare frog and monarch: one similarity and one difference.
W3. Give a counterexample to “all egg-layers are birds”.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: compare a pair
pupilPages.intro: Use cards F and M. Word bank: eggs / larva / pupa / adult.

blocks.prompt: S1. Which stage occurs in both routes?
S2. Complete: Both have a ____ stage. The monarch has a ____ ; the common frog does not.
S3. Put these monarch stages in order: adult, egg, pupa, caterpillar.
S4. A platypus lays eggs. Is it a bird?
S5. Explain why “all egg-layers are birds” is wrong. Name one card.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: feature table
pupilPages.intro: Use the same question for each animal.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the table using the species cards.
N2. Compare frog and monarch using one similarity and one difference.
N3. Compare platypus and robin using egg-laying and feeding of young.
N4. Correct “all egg-layers are birds”. Explain why four species do not describe every animal.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: challenge the rules
pupilPages.intro: A strong claim stays within the evidence.

blocks.prompt: T1. Write a comparison of two species using three matched features.
T2. Evaluate “all larvae become pupae” using the frog and monarch cards.
T3. Evaluate “all mammals give live birth”. Identify a counterexample and its classification evidence.
T4. A fifth species has no feeding information. Can you record “no parental feeding”? Explain a better entry.
E1. Give one similarity between frog and monarch cycles.
E2. Give one difference in their stages.
E3. Give a counterexample to “all egg-layers are birds”. Explain.
E4. Does an adult turn into its own egg? Explain the cycle arrow.
Reflection. Which comparison question would you investigate next?

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: Reproduce; a named animal with a larva such as frog or monarch; no, the next generation contains new individuals.

answers.label: W1–W3
answers.answer: W1 pupa: monarch yes, other three no; milk: platypus yes, other three no. Groups change because the feature changes. W2 both eggs/larvae; monarch has pupa and frog does not. W3 frog, monarch or platypus is a non-bird egg-layer; platypus is a mammal.

answers.label: Hinge A–C
answers.answer: A false: same feature is not identical cycle. B correct. C false: platypus is an egg-laying mammal.

answers.label: S1–S5
answers.answer: S1 egg. S2 larva; pupa. S3 egg→caterpillar→pupa→adult. S4 no, mammal. S5 name a non-bird egg-layer and state that this contradicts all egg-layers being birds.

answers.label: N1–N4
answers.answer: N1 frog no/no; monarch yes/no; platypus no/yes; robin no/no. N2 both eggs or larvae, but pupa only monarch. N3 both lay eggs; platypus young receive milk whereas robin chicks receive other food from parents. N4 valid counterexample; a sample of four cannot establish every possible animal life cycle.

answers.label: T1–T4
answers.answer: T1 three accurately matched features, for example frog and monarch: egg location pond versus milkweed, larvae both, pupa absent versus present. T2 false: tadpoles are larvae but no pupa follows. T3 false: platypus lays eggs and feeds young milk. T4 missing information is not evidence of absence; record not supplied/unknown and seek a reliable source.

answers.label: E1–E4 / assessment
answers.answer: E1 eggs or larvae. E2 pupa only monarch. E3 named correct non-bird case and contradiction. E4 adults produce new offspring, not themselves becoming eggs. Secure: matched comparison and valid counterexample; re-teach vague differences by selecting one common feature question. Reflection accepts a relevant evidence question.

teacherNotes: 40 minutes: opening 2; retrieval 3; I do 8; We do 8; hinge 3; You do 10; review 4; exit 2. Zero-minute slides share their stage time.
Supply shared page 1, one selected route page 2, 3 or 4, and page 5. Do not require all three routes. An independent spoken explanation can be recorded verbatim by an adult.

The comparison extends the earlier life-cycle archive through new comparison questions and a matched-feature matrix. It intentionally revisits species knowledge rather than claiming untouched content.
Interactive sorting decisions map to W1–W3; paper cards support the same predict, check and explain cycle.
